extracted.intended_audience: general readers / literary audience (readers of North American Review; Mark Twain enthusiasts)
extracted.subtask_description: An excerpt of Mark Twain's autobiographical chapters (anecdotes, club recollections, and moral observations) as published in the North American Review; literary memoir prose rather than an instructional guideline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monday Evening Club meeting rules/format
rubrics_metrics.description: Description of the Club's membership, season, and meeting structure: "The Monday Evening Club still exists. ... It was founded about forty-five years ago ... The membership was restricted, in those days, to eighteen--possibly twenty. The meetings began about the 1st of October and were held in the private houses of the members every fortnight thereafter throughout the cold months until the 1st of May."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes procedural details and expectations for how the club runs (private houses, seasonal schedule, fortnightly meetings). Useful as a procedural standard for organizing similar literary/salon meetings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Essayist selection, order, and presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Essayists choose their own subject and present in alphabetical order through the season: "The essayists followed each other in alphabetical order through the season. The essayist could choose his own subject and talk twenty minutes on it, from MS. or orally, according to his preference."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifies presentation rights (topic choice), order (alphabetical rotation), and permitted formats (manuscript or oral). Also sets an expected talk length (twenty minutes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Discussion participation limits and audience etiquette
rubrics_metrics.description: After the essay there is a timed discussion and rules about audience presence: "Then the discussion followed, and each member present was allowed ten minutes in which to express his views. The wives of these people were always present. It was their privilege. It was also their privilege to keep still; they were not allowed to throw any light upon the discussion."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives explicit limits for discussion participation (ten minutes per member) and notes the social etiquette expected of non-speaking attendees (wives present but not permitted to speak). Also records supper timing (began at ten o'clock; company broke up at midnight).

rubrics_metrics.name: Anecdote/storytelling caution: beware of 'embroidery' from repetition
rubrics_metrics.description: A caution about repeated telling of tales leading to embellishment: examples include the narrator's mother's phrase about 'embroidery' and Dr. Burton's admonition after analyzing a repeatedly told tale: "I found that its proportions were now, as nearly as I could make out, one part fact, straight fact, fact pure and undiluted, golden fact, and twenty-four parts embroidery."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical guidance for storytellers: repeated retelling tends to accumulate embellishments and can degrade the tale's factual integrity and the teller's confidence; the conservative remedy offered is to stop retelling to avoid further 'embroidery.' Also includes narrator's earlier remark that his mother 'discount[s] him thirty per cent. for embroidery.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Designing bounties/incentives: beware perverse effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Observation about unintended consequences of bounty schemes, illustrated by the household fly-bounty anecdote: paying for dead flies led children to create a 'Fly Trust' and hire neighborhood children to produce flies for payment. Quotation: "The best way to increase wolves in America, rabbits in Australia, and snakes in India, is to pay a bounty on their scalps."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implied policy guideline: incentives such as bounties can create perverse behaviors and artificial supply; designers should foresee and guard against gaming and unintended economic incentives.
